newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan team leaves for Washington to meet IMF.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan team leaves for Washington to meet IMF.

text.p: Pakistani economic officials left for Washington on Sunday to discuss an emergency package with the International Monetary Fund, an official said.

The official, who asked not to be named, said Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's economic adviser, Shahid Hassan Khan, accompanied by State (central) Bank of Pakistan governor Muhammad Yaqub and finance ministry officials, would brief the IMF on Pakistan's latest proposals to rescue the economy.
Conspicuously absent from the delegation was Bhutto's top finance adviser V.A. Jafarey, who has acted as finance minister in all but name since her government was formed in 1993.
There was no immediate word on why Jafarey, who has headed the Pakistani team in earlier negotiations with the IMF, was staying in Islamabad. He could not be reached for comment.
The government said on Thursday it had approved an outline deal with the IMF, but gave no details of the measures to reduce Pakistan's yawning current account and budget deficits.

Official sources said the government had modified the IMF proposals and wanted to discuss the changes with the fund before announcing anything in Pakistan. One source said the government had decided to cut development spending, but gave no figures.

Bhutto met President Farooq Leghari and chief ministers of all of Pakistan's four provinces on Sunday to discuss the package, designed to meet IMF conditions for a resumption of payments on a stalled $600 million standby loan, officials said.
They said the talks focused on how to achieve effective implementation of agricultural income tax, a key IMF demand.
Three provinces passed legislation in June 1994 to introduce agricultural income tax, but provincial government officials say resistance from big landowners has kept receipts negligible.
Populous Punjab province, Pakistan's agricultural powerhouse, has not even introduced the tax due to opposition from the rich landowners who dominate the provincial assembly.
The IMF has held up disbursements of a $600 million standby loan because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed reforms and confusion over the 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
It cannot disburse the delayed payments until a mission has visited Pakistan and completed a review of the economy.
The IMF has previously asked Pakistan to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from anywhere between five and six percent in fiscal 1995/96.
